title: Individual Rights
summary: Rights as principles that sanction freedom of action in a social context.

lessons.title: What a right is
lessons.objective: Identify a right as a principle that sanctions a person's freedom of action.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what is a right?

choices.text: A principle that sanctions freedom of action
A private wish that others must fulfill
A feeling that something is unfair
A count of how people usually behave

feedback.note: A right is a principle. It sanctions freedom of action. It is not a mood, a wish, or a statistic.

exercises.prompt: What does a right sanction?

choices.text: Freedom of action
A guaranteed share of other people's goods
Praise from the group
Success no matter what you do

feedback.note: The thing sanctioned is freedom of action, not a promised outcome or a claim on someone else's product.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to what it is in this unit.

pairs.right: A principle that sanctions freedom of action

feedback.note: Keep the three pieces together: a principle, freedom of action, and a social context.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit's definition.

feedback.note: The word that belongs here is freedom. Approval, wealth, and obedience are not what the principle sanctions.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Call it a principle. A privilege is granted and can be withdrawn. A mood is not a moral standard.

exercises.prompt: Which statement fits this unit?

choices.text: A right sanctions action; it does not hand you a result
A right is a gift the majority may cancel at will
A right appears whenever someone feels a need
A right is a rule you set only for yourself in private

feedback.note: Sanction means the principle authorizes the action. It does not promise that the action will succeed.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the idea it confuses with a right.

pairs.right: A custom, not a sanction of action

pairs.left: I want someone else to provide it
pairs.right: A claim on others, not freedom of action

feedback.note: Feelings, customs, and demands on other people are not the definition of a right.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two key words.

feedback.note: Principle and action are the two words. A feeling is not a principle, and a reward is not the freedom the principle sanctions.

exercises.prompt: Sanction, as used here, means:

choices.text: The principle authorizes that kind of action
The group punishes the action
Someone else must pay for the action
The action must stay secret

feedback.note: To sanction freedom of action is to treat that freedom as morally authorized, not as something to punish, fund, or hide.

lessons.title: A social context
lessons.objective: Place rights among people, not in a person's dealings with nature or with himself alone.

exercises.prompt: Where do rights apply?

choices.text: In a social context, among people
In a person's struggle with nature
Only in a life with no other people
Only inside private wishes

feedback.note: The summary places rights in a social context. They are principles for how people may act toward one another.

exercises.prompt: A storm destroys a crop. Is that a violation of rights?

choices.text: No. Nature is not a person in a social context
Yes. Any loss is a rights violation
Only if the farmer voted against storms
Yes, if the crop was valuable

feedback.note: Rights govern action among people. A natural event is not another person's action.

exercises.prompt: Match each setting to whether rights are the issue.

pairs.left: How one person may act toward another
pairs.right: A social context, so rights apply

pairs.left: How a person deals with weather or disease
A promise a person makes only to himself
pairs.right: Private, not a right against others

feedback.note: Use the social test. If no other person is involved as an actor, the question is not a question of rights.

exercises.prompt: Complete the summary phrase.

parts.text: Rights sanction freedom of action in a

feedback.note: The context is social. Private plans, natural events, and money totals are not the context the principle names.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Among people is the social context. Storms and solitude do not create a rights question by themselves.

exercises.prompt: Why does the unit mention a social context?

choices.text: Rights set terms for action between people
Rights guarantee a win against nature
Rights replace a person's own judgment
Rights exist only inside clubs and parties

feedback.note: The social context is the setting in which one person's action can conflict with another's. That is where the principle is needed.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to the right category.

pairs.left: May she stop him from speaking?
Will the river flood the field?

pairs.right: A question for his own judgment

feedback.note: Only the first question is about one person's action toward another. The others stay outside the social principle.

exercises.prompt: Fill the missing idea.

parts.text: , there is no social context for rights.

feedback.note: People are required for the social context. Tools, moods, and prices do not by themselves make a rights question.

exercises.prompt: Two neighbors disagree about a fence line. Why can rights be relevant?

choices.text: The dispute is between people about action
Land itself has rights
Older opinions always become rights
The louder neighbor defines the right

feedback.note: A fence dispute is social: it is about what each person may do. Volume and age do not create the principle.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Social context means people acting in relation to one another. Weather is outside that relation.

lessons.title: Freedom of action
lessons.objective: Distinguish the freedom a right sanctions from a claim on other people's effort or goods.

exercises.prompt: A right to act freely is which of these?

choices.text: Sanction to take your own action
A right to be served by someone else
A right to another person's paycheck
A right to succeed

feedback.note: Freedom of action is about what you may do. It is not a ticket to someone else's labor, money, or success.

exercises.prompt: Which demand goes beyond freedom of action?

choices.text: Others must build and give you a house
You may build a house on your own terms with your own means
You may offer to trade for a house
You may keep what you have produced

feedback.note: Building, trading, and keeping are actions you take. Requiring others to supply a house turns their action into your claim.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement to the right label.

pairs.left: He may offer his work for pay

feedback.note: Speaking and offering are the person's own actions. Agreement and hiring are other people's actions, so they are not owed as rights.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

feedback.note: Action is what the principle sanctions for you. Another person's effort stays that person's to choose.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Freedom of action and a claim on others are different ideas. Do not swap them.

exercises.prompt: You are free to seek medical care. What does that freedom not include?

choices.text: A doctor's duty to treat you without his choice
Your freedom to ask a doctor
Your freedom to pay for care
Your freedom to study medicine

feedback.note: Asking, paying, and learning are your actions. Compelling the doctor's action is a claim on him, not your freedom of action.

exercises.prompt: Match the freedom to what it leaves open.

pairs.right: No one must carry you there

feedback.note: Each freedom sanctions your action and leaves other people free to act or not act in response.

exercises.prompt: Fill the blank.

parts.text: A right does not entitle you to the

feedback.note: The product of someone else's work is not what a right sanctions. Your freedom is to act, including to produce or to trade.

exercises.prompt: Which pair is consistent with this lesson?

choices.text: You may create; others may decline to buy
You may create; others must buy
You may not create unless a committee agrees first
Others own the result of your effort by right

feedback.note: Creation is your action. Buying is theirs. A right keeps both freedoms instead of assigning one person's effort to the other.

lessons.title: Not a permission
lessons.objective: Contrast a right with a permission or privilege that others can grant or withdraw.

exercises.prompt: How does a right differ from a permission?

choices.text: A right is a moral principle, not a favor someone grants
They are the same thing
A right exists only after a vote creates it
A right is a gift that expires when the giver changes his mind

feedback.note: A permission depends on the person who gives it. A right, in this unit, is a principle that sanctions action, not a favor.

exercises.prompt: A committee says you may speak only on Tuesdays. That rule treats speech as:

choices.text: A permission the committee can narrow
A right the committee discovered
A fact about nature
Proof that need creates rights

feedback.note: If a group can hand the action out or take it back, the group is treating it as a permission, not recognizing a right.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to the name.

pairs.left: Leave to act, given and revocable by others
A special advantage handed to some people

feedback.note: Rights are principles. Permissions and privileges are grants. Do not use the three words as synonyms.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

parts.text: . A right is not that kind of grant.

feedback.note: Withdrawn marks the grant. A right is not created by the same act that can cancel it.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: The sentence draws the contrast directly. A favor and a vote are ways permissions get handed out, not what a right is.

exercises.prompt: If a right were only a privilege, what would follow?

choices.text: Whoever holds power could cancel the freedom
The freedom would be safer
Nothing would change
Nature would have to obey the privilege

feedback.note: A privilege lives at the discretion of the grantor. Treating freedom that way drops the idea of a sanctioning principle.

exercises.prompt: Match the wording to the idea it expresses.

pairs.left: You have a right to work
Only members of this group may trade

feedback.note: Allow and only-some are grant language. A right is the principle that sanctions the action, not a club benefit.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks.

feedback.note: Grant versus principle is the contrast. A storm and a habit do not define either term.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, The group gave you your rights, so the group may take them back. What is the mistake?

choices.text: It treats a right as a revocable permission
There is no mistake
It confuses rights with the weather
It uses the wrong count of people

feedback.note: Giving and taking back are the logic of permissions. This unit defines a right as a principle, not as something the group lends.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Granted is the mark of a permission. Do not attach that verb to the definition of a right.

lessons.title: Rights as principles
lessons.objective: Treat rights as moral principles that set a standard, not as wishes, customs, or majority votes.

exercises.prompt: As a principle, a right functions as:

choices.text: A standard for judging action in a social context
Whatever the latest poll prefers
Whatever people have always done
Whatever someone wants at the moment

feedback.note: A principle is a standard you can apply. Polls, habits, and momentary wants do not replace it.

exercises.prompt: A majority wants to silence a speaker. What does the principle say about that wish?

choices.text: A wish, even a majority wish, is not itself a right
The larger number creates the right
Only an old custom can judge the wish
The wish is a right if it is shouted

feedback.note: Numbers do not turn a wish into a principle. The right still sanctions the speaker's freedom of action.

exercises.prompt: Match each source to why it is not the definition of a right.

pairs.right: Habit is not a moral sanction
A count is not the standard

feedback.note: Wishes, customs, and votes can be described. None of them is the principle that sanctions freedom of action.

exercises.prompt: Complete the lesson claim.

parts.text: , so it can judge a custom instead of merely copying it.

feedback.note: Because it is a principle, the right is a standard for custom. It is not identical with the custom.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: Standard is the job of a principle. Fashion and a poll record what people happen to prefer.

exercises.prompt: Which question uses a right as a principle?

choices.text: Does this action stay within the freedom the principle sanctions?
How many people like this action?
Did our grandparents do this?
Do I feel like doing this?

feedback.note: The principle asks whether the action is sanctioned. Popularity, ancestry, and mood ask different questions.

exercises.prompt: Match the test to the mistake it avoids.

pairs.left: Check the principle, not the wish
pairs.right: Avoids treating desire as a right

pairs.left: Check the principle, not the custom
pairs.right: Avoids treating habit as a right

pairs.left: Check the principle, not the head count
pairs.right: Avoids treating a vote as a right

feedback.note: Each test keeps the right in the role of a standard rather than a report of what people want, repeat, or vote.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two blanks.

feedback.note: Principles versus wishes is the contrast of this lesson. Storms and tools belong to other topics.

exercises.prompt: A long-standing custom forbids a peaceful trade. What can a right do that the custom cannot?

choices.text: Serve as a standard that judges the custom
Only repeat the custom
End every disagreement by itself
Set the price of the trade

feedback.note: The principle can stand against the custom because it sanctions freedom of action. It does not become a price list or a machine that ends every dispute.

exercises.prompt: Build the study sentence.

feedback.note: A vote can record a decision. It does not take the place of the principle that sanctions freedom of action.
